cim: As states move quickly to govern AI, dedicated oversight remains a challenge
kihagyva: P3: 52 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: As states move quickly to govern AI, dedicated oversight remains a challenge
szoveg_eredeti:
State governments are rapidly creating dedicated leadership roles to oversee artificial intelligence. But many of those officials lack the staffing, funding and authority needed to manage the technology across government agencies, according to a new report by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers.

The report, published Tuesday, surveyed 33 states and territories to examine how governments are organizing AI leadership, developing governance policies and preparing employees to use the technology.

The findings show how quickly AI oversight has become a priority for state technology offices, but suggests that establishing an AI leadership position is only the first step.

“When NASCIO first started tracking in 2023, less than 20 percent of states had a state chief artificial intelligence officer or a similar title,” the report states. “Just three years later, at least 46 states have identified at least one person tasked with directing artificial intelligence and by our count 25 states have someone with AI in their title. It seems the role is growing as fast as the technology itself.”

But those positions are still evolving. According to the report, 76% percent of survey respondents said they were the first person to hold their role as currently defined in their state. Furthermore, most positions were established through a directive from the state CIO rather than legislation or an executive order.

The report also found that AI leadership does not always come with the authority to establish or enforce statewide policies. While 72% of respondents said they have jurisdiction over all executive branch agencies, only 44% have the authority to independently establish enterprise AI policies and standards. Another 16% share that responsibility with another entity and just over half said they have the power to enforce compliance with those policies.

Governance is growing, but resources lag

States have made progress establishing rules for how government employees and agencies can use AI in recent years, the report found.

Ninety-seven percent of survey respondents said their states have developed AI policies or guidance, while 83% have created processes for agencies to submit proposed AI use cases for review. The National Institute of Standards and Technology’s AI Risk Management Framework, released in 2023, was the most commonly used governance model, cited by roughly 75% of respondents. The framework provides guidance for identifying and managing potential risks associated with AI systems, including concerns about accuracy, privacy security and bias.

Other common practices include statewide employee training, AI governance committees and inventories documenting how agencies are using AI.

In February, Washington, D.C., became the first major U.S. city to mandate AI training for all employees and contractors. The free training program covers prompting basics, responsible innovation and recognizing deepfakes. Shortly after, New York expanded its AI training resources in April to the state’s entire workforce of more than 100,000 employees following a pilot program involving eight agencies.

Similarly, San José, California, has trained over 1,000 municipal employees since 2024 through an AI upskilling program aimed at helping workers develop tools to address operational challenges. In the two years since it launched, the initiative has produced AI applications across multiple city departments, including a tool that automatically verifies emergency vehicles are equipped before deployment, a system that reviews contractor submissions to identify missing information and drafts response emails, and an AI assistant that evaluates projects that further San José’s goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2030, among others.

Still, the resources available to oversee these programs vary. Fifty-six percent of respondents said their states do not have dedicated AI budgets and 75% identified insufficient staffing as one of their biggest challenges.

“Chief AI officers would benefit from having full authority to establish and enforce enterprise AI standards,” the report states. “This would reduce agency and staff burden, increase interagency cooperation and unify agencies in the state.”

The report’s findings build on NASCIO’s 2026 State CIO Survey, which found that 78% of state CIOs now have an AI governance framework, up from 65% in 2025. AI also ranked as the top technology priority among state CIOs for the first time this year.

Despite the obstacles, states are finding ways to translate those policies into practice. California has expanded oversight of AI vendors and advances plans for independent safety audits. Vermont has also begun integrating AI governance into its broader data strategy and employee training programs.

Looking ahead, the report found that state AI leaders expect their responsibilities to expand as governments move beyond generative AI tools that produce text and images toward agentic AI systems capable of completing tasks and taking actions with less human involvement.

Ninety percent of respondents said agentic AI would consume significantly more of their time over the next three years, with workforce transformation and scaling AI across agencies also major anticipated priorities.

NASCIO recommends that states give AI leaders clearly defined authority, invest in dedicated staffing and sustainable funding efforts, strengthen collaboration among technology, privacy and cybersecurity teams, and expand employee training.

“With the right foundation, states can navigate the evolving risks and challenges of AI while harnessing its potential to improve government operations and the services they provide to the public,” the report concludes.
